passages.happening:
As the number of disciples grows, a complaint arises. “The Grecian Jews among them began to grumble against the Hebraic Jews because their widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution of food” (verse 1).

The Twelve call the whole community together. “It is unacceptable for us to neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables” (verse 2). So they ask the believers to choose seven men “full of the Spirit and wisdom” (verse 3) to take charge of this work, while the apostles give themselves “to prayer and to the ministry of the word” (verse 4).

The whole group is pleased. They choose Stephen, “a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit”, and Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas from Antioch, a convert to Judaism (verse 5). The apostles pray and lay their hands on them.

“So the word of God continued to spread. The number of disciples in Jerusalem grew rapidly, and a great number of priests became obedient to the faith” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
All the believers here are Jews. The difference between the two groups is language and background. The ‘Grecian Jews’, often called Hellenists, spoke Greek; many had been born or raised in Jewish communities around the Mediterranean and had come to live in Jerusalem. The ‘Hebraic Jews’ were mostly from the land itself and spoke Aramaic, the local language, and could read the Hebrew Scriptures. Both were fully Jewish. But language divides people easily, and the Greek-speakers' widows were being missed.

Widows in the ancient world were among the most exposed people there were. Without a husband's income, and often far from family, many had nothing. Widows who had come from abroad to live near the temple would have had few relatives in the city. The church had taken on a daily share of food for them, and it was failing some of them.

Look at the names of the seven. All are Greek names. The church seems to have chosen men from the very group that felt left out. Nicolas was not even born a Jew; he was a Gentile from Antioch who had become a Jew, and then a believer. Around AD 180 Irenaeus thought a sect called the Nicolaitans, condemned in Revelation 2:6, took its name from this Nicolas; many scholars doubt the link.

The apostles do not think serving tables is beneath anyone. Jesus had said, “I am among you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). They simply see that they cannot do everything, and that others are gifted for this.
passages.ot:
The Law commands care for widows again and again: “You must not mistreat any widow or orphan” (Exodus 22:22); God “executes justice for the fatherless and widow” (Deuteronomy 10:18). The prophets made it a test of true faith: “Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow” (Isaiah 1:17).

Sharing the work has an old pattern too. When Moses was worn out, his father-in-law told him to choose capable men to share the load, “so that your load may be lightened as they share it with you” (Exodus 18:22).

Laying on hands was how Moses passed on a charge to Joshua: “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man with the Spirit in him, and lay your hands on him” (Numbers 27:18). It marked a person as sent and blessed for a task.
passages.hard:
Were the seven the first deacons? Luke never calls them deacons, though he uses the related Greek word for their ‘service’ and for ‘waiting on’ tables. From early times many Christians have seen them as the first deacons, the office named in Philippians 1:1 and described in 1 Timothy 3:8-13. Others think they were a group chosen for one problem, more like helpers of the apostles or leaders among the Greek-speaking believers. They note that Stephen and Philip are soon preaching, not handing out food, and that Philip is later called ‘the evangelist’, ‘one of the Seven’ (21:8).

Churches with different kinds of leadership, led by bishops, by elders, or by the congregation, each find support for their practice here: the apostles propose and lay on hands, and the whole community chooses. These are questions on which faithful churches differ, and these notes do not settle them. What the passage shows plainly is a way of working: a complaint is heard and not dismissed, the people affected are given a voice, practical care is treated as spiritual work, and the people chosen must be of proven character.
passages.asks: The first church fight in Acts was about food and fairness, and it was settled by listening, sharing the work and trusting the people who had been overlooked. Ask who might be overlooked in your church, perhaps because they speak differently or come from somewhere else. And ask whether you treat practical service as less spiritual than prayer and preaching. The apostles did not.

passages.t: Stephen, full of grace and power, accused
passages.happening:
“Now Stephen, who was full of grace and power, was performing great wonders and signs among the people” (verse 8).

Opposition comes from the Synagogue of the Freedmen, with men from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia. They argue with Stephen, “but they could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke” (verse 10).

So they put men up to say, “We heard Stephen speak words of blasphemy against Moses and against God” (verse 11). They stir up the people, the elders and the teachers of the law, seize Stephen and bring him before the council. False witnesses say, “This man never stops speaking against this holy place and against the law” (verse 13), and that he said Jesus of Nazareth will destroy the temple and change the customs Moses gave.

“All who were sitting in the Sanhedrin looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
‘Freedmen’ is a Latin word in Greek dress, libertini: people who had been slaves and were set free, or their children. Many think this synagogue was formed by Jews whose families had been taken to Rome as captives, after the Roman general Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, and later freed; others suggest other origins. Either way, it was a Greek-speaking synagogue of Jews from abroad, from North Africa (Cyrene and Alexandria) and from what is now Turkey (Cilicia and Asia).

A Greek inscription found in Jerusalem in 1913 tells of a synagogue built by a priest named Theodotus ‘for the reading of the law and for the teaching of the commandments’, with rooms for visitors from abroad. Some have connected it with a synagogue like this one, but the link is uncertain.

Cilicia is worth noticing. It was the home province of Saul of Tarsus, who will appear at the end of the next chapter. He may have been among those who argued with Stephen, though Luke does not say so.

Stephen's opponents are Greek-speaking Jews like himself. This is an argument inside a family. Their charge is that he spoke against the temple and the law, the two great signs of God's presence and will. Those were the most serious charges a Jew could face.
passages.ot: Stephen's shining face recalls Moses. When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the law, “his face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD” (Exodus 34:29), and the people were afraid to come near. The man accused of speaking against Moses looks, to his judges, like Moses himself.
passages.hard:
The charges against Stephen echo the charges against Jesus. At Jesus' trial too, false witnesses said, “We heard Him say, ‘I will destroy this man-made temple’” (Mark 14:58). Luke tells Stephen's story so that the reader sees the disciple walking his Lord's road: the council, the false witnesses, the charge about the temple, and soon a death with a prayer for his killers.

The charges were false in the way they were put, but they were not made up from nothing. Stephen does seem to have taught that God's presence was not tied to the temple, as his speech in the next chapter shows. Readers have long asked how far that was faithful to Jesus and to Israel's prophets. Stephen's answer will be that it was exactly what the prophets had said.
passages.asks: Stephen's opponents could not answer him, so they twisted his words. Ask how you respond when you lose an argument: with honesty, or by making the other person sound worse than he is. And notice that the man described as full of grace, wisdom, faith and power was chosen first to serve food to widows.
